extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, philosophers of science, historians of mathematics, cognitive scientists, and mathematicians interested in foundations and mathematical practice
extracted.subtask_description: A survey-style encyclopedia entry summarizing approaches, methodological commitments, and key evaluative themes in the philosophy of mathematical practice (PMP). It outlines what counts as the domain of PMP, how to study it, and the epistemic virtues and issues used to evaluate mathematical work and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Areas of Mathematics (scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: PMP considers all areas of mathematics to be under its purview rather than restricting attention to arithmetic, set theory, and logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry argues that focusing only on arithmetic and set theory 'idealises too much' and loses opportunities for philosophical analysis; to study topics like visualization and diagrammatic reasoning one must consider geometry, topology, analysis, algebra, combinatorics, etc. PMP therefore treats mathematics as multiform and urges attention to transversal themes across areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects Doing Mathematics (agents & history)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate the actual subjects (agents) doing mathematics, including their cognitive features, historical situatedness, and social roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than assuming highly idealized, logically omniscient agents, PMP gives special attention to history, human cognitive architecture, social practices, and how these affect mathematical development. This includes engaging with cognitive psychology, social epistemology (testimony, trust, group knowledge), and historical case studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological stance: bottom-up vs top-down
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer drawing philosophical conclusions from detailed case studies (bottom-up) rather than supplying only general, top-down characterizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry contrasts top-down accounts of explanation (e.g., Steiner, Kitcher) with PMP's bottom-up critiques and recommends basing accounts on analyses of real proofs and episodes. Different branches of PMP vary in how strongly they adopt bottom-up methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative vs Descriptive integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which normative standards for mathematics should be informed by descriptive study of actual mathematical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PMP ranges from fully descriptive projects to approaches that integrate descriptive evidence into normative proposals. Examples: Tymoczko's norms for proofs attend to practice; Easwaran suggests proofs should be 'transferable'; De Toffoli argues proofs should be 'shareable.' The entry recommends calibrating normative claims with how mathematics is actually done.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice: product vs process (product/process ambiguity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify whether 'practice' means the products of mathematics (proofs, explanations, diagrams) or the processes and activities of doing mathematics; treat this as a spectrum rather than a dichotomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some PMP work focuses on products (arguments, proofs) whereas other work emphasizes processes, communities, and mathematical culture. Both ends have implications for what counts as appropriate philosophical investigation and evaluation criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof norms: transferability
rubrics_metrics.description: A suggested norm that mathematical proofs should be 'transferable' — i.e., capable of being communicated in ways that enable others to grasp and use them (Easwaran).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transferability is presented as a practice-informed norm: proofs should be presented so they can be taken up by others. This interacts with debates over formal vs informal proofs and with questions raised by computer-assisted proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof norms: shareability
rubrics_metrics.description: A suggested norm that proofs should be 'shareable'—able to be communicated and checked by members of the mathematical community (De Toffoli).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shareability underscores social epistemic dimensions and supports evaluating proofs in terms of how they are adopted, transmitted, and collectively validated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic Virtue: Purity of Methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Purity of methods (e.g., keeping methods within a single subdiscipline) is an epistemic value evaluated in mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PMP examines why purity is valued, its trade-offs, and debates about 'impurity' (mixing methods) in contemporary mathematics. Work by Lehet and others on impurity is discussed as an evaluative axis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic Virtue: Mathematical Explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical explanation is a central epistemic desideratum, with multiple competing accounts and an emphasis that accounts should be sensitive to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry surveys accounts (Steiner's characteristic property, Kitcher's unification) and documents criticisms from practice-oriented studies. It recommends bottom-up analyses of explanation and notes empirical and conceptual work on what functions as an explanation in mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic Virtue: Mathematical Rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigor is a key evaluative standard, but its meaning and role are contested (formal rigor vs informal practices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PMP analyzes the nature and value of rigor, the relation between informal proofs and formal proofs, and contemporary debates (e.g., the role of large-scale collaborations, computer-assisted proofs). References include Tymoczko, Tanswell, Pawlowski & Zahidi, and debates about how much formalization is required for epistemic warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams and Visualization (diagrammatic reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrammatic reasoning and visualization are legitimate epistemic resources and must be evaluated for how they function and justify mathematical claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry highlights historical and contemporary studies of diagrams (Euclid, Manders, Netz), discusses their epistemic roles, and urges philosophers to account for the discipline-specific 'controls' that make diagrammatic reasoning reliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological Developments: computer-assisted proofs and AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how computational tools (computer-assisted proofs, automated theorem proving, AI) affect the nature, acceptability, and epistemic evaluation of proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples such as the Appel–Haken 4-color theorem proof are discussed as pressuring traditional views that proofs must be surveyable by an individual; contemporary work on autoformalization and AI raises new questions about correctness, verification, and epistemic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative Foundations and axiom choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical assessment of alternative foundations (category theory, homotopy type theory) and the rationale for adopting new axioms or foundational frameworks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PMP treats foundational choices as partly motivated by mathematical practice and development. Issues include whether category theory can serve as a foundation, debates over axioms (Axiom of Choice, Continuum Hypothesis, large cardinals), and the philosophical implications of homotopy type theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Epistemic Criteria (trust, testimony, group knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate mathematical knowledge and justification in terms of social-epistemic processes: trust, testimony, group knowledge, division of cognitive labor, epistemic injustice and exclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry emphasizes research applying social epistemology to mathematics (testimony, group justification, trust, epistemic exclusions/injustice). These serve as criteria for understanding how mathematical results are validated and circulated in communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical relevance as evidential resource
rubrics_metrics.description: Use historical case studies to inform philosophical accounts of mathematical growth, discovery, and justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos' Proofs and Refutations is cited as a paradigm: history can reveal quasi-empirical, fallible development of mathematics and inform debates about rigor, progress, and explanation. PMP recommends integrating detailed historical analyses into philosophical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive and embodied approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate cognitive science and embodied cognition findings when evaluating mathematical practice, notation, and reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works by Lakoff & Núñez, Giaquinto, Dehaene, and others illustrate how cognitive architecture, perception, and embodiment inform mathematical concepts, notation design, and diagrammatic reasoning; such empirical results provide evidence for epistemic claims about practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Notation: design principles and trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate mathematical notation by its design principles, trade-offs, expressiveness, and impact on reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry references analyses of notation (Schlimm on Begriffsschrift, works on notation trade-offs) and recommends assessing notations for cognitive affordances, clarity, and their role in mathematical communication and discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic values beyond access to abstract objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize values like fruitfulness, evidence, understanding, explanation, and fit as legitimate epistemic goals in mathematics distinct from the problem of access to abstract objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PMP expands the epistemology of mathematics to include these orthogonal values; evaluations should consider whether mathematical work promotes understanding, explanatory depth, fruitfulness, and conceptual fit rather than only ontological access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological pluralism and positioning relative to foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: Position research along an ecumenical–anti-foundationalist axis, acknowledging complementarity or opposition to traditional foundational projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some PMP scholars emphasize continuity with foundational projects (ecumenical), others reject foundations as central (anti-foundationalist). The entry suggests that methodological choices determine which evaluative criteria are privileged and that plural approaches are common.
